paragraph: In Example 1, we demonstrated an application of fair set cover for Team of Experts Formation. To demonstrate the application-spanof our formulation, in the following, we briefly mention a few more applications. Eqal Base-rate in representative data sets. An equal base rate is defined as having an equal number of objects for different subgroups in the data set [ 30]. Satisfying equal base-rate is im- portant for satisfying multiple fairness metrics in down-stream machine learning task. Consider the schema of a dataset of individ- ual records (e.g., Chicago breast-cancer examination data), with a set of attributes x={x1,···,xη}, where dom(xi)>1is the domain ofxi. In order to ensure representativeness in the data, suppose we would like to collect a minimal set that contains at least one instance from all possible level- lvalue combinations. A level- l combination is a value-combination containing lattributes in x. Each individual belongs to a demographic group (e.g., White ,Black ). In order to reduce potential unfairnesses for various groups (e.g., Chicago breast-cancer detection disparities [ 23]), it is required to satisfy equal base-rate in the dataset. This is an instance of fair set cover, where each row (individual record) in the data set, covers all level-lcombinations it matches with. Business license distribution. Issuing a minimum number of business licences (e.g., cannabis dispensary) while covering the population of a city is a challenging task for the City Office. Each business location covers regions within a certain (travel time) range. Besides coverage, equity is a critical constraint in these settings. For example, disparity against Black -owned cannabis dispensaries in Chicago is a well-known issue [ 48]. Formulating and solving this problem as a fair set cover instance will resolve the disparity issues. In Social Networks a similar application is influencer selec- tion, where companies would like to select a small set of “innflu- encers” to reach out to their target application. Specifically, once an influencer (aka content creator) post a content about a product, their followers view it. However, the company might also want to send their products to a diverse set of influencers, to prevent vi- sual biases in their advertisement [ 34]. Each influencer has a "cost" which is the amount of money that they should get to advertise a product. The company should minimize the advertising budget so the problem is mapped to the fair weighted set cover problem.

Hardness and Assumption. It is straightforward to show that FSC is NP-Complete. Recently, Barnabò et al. [ 5] showed that FSC cannot be approximated with any sublinear approximation factor in polynomial time unless P=NP. However, if there are enough sets from each group, then in the next sections we design efficient algorithms with provable approximation guarantees. More formally, for the FSC problem, we assume that every group contains at least Ω(logn)|X∗| ksets. For simplicity, in the next sections we also as- sume that every group has the same number of sets, i.e., for every group gjit holds that mj=m.

We first describe a naive algorithm for the FSC problem with large approximation ratio. We execute the well-known greedy algorithm for the standard set cover problem (its pseudocode is shown in the technical report [ 14]) and letXbe the set cover we get. If Xdoes not satisfy the fairness requirements, we arbitrarily add the minimal number of sets from each color to equalize the number of sets from each color in our final cover. The pseudocode is shown in the technical report [14]. Lemma 1. There exists a(︁k(lnn+1))︁-approximation algorithm for the FSC problem that runs in O(m·k·n)time.

In this subsection we propose an algorithm for the FSC problem whose approximation ratio does not depend onk. For simplicity of explanation, we describe our algorithm for the case we have only two demographic groups, i.e., G={g1,g2}. In the end, our algorithm can be extended almost verbatim to k>2groups. LetX=∅be the cover we construct and let U−=Ube the set of uncovered elements. We repeat the following steps until U−=∅. In each iteration, we find the pair of sets(SA,SB)such that i) setsSA,SBcover the maximum number of uncovered elements, i.e.,U−∩(SA∪SB)is maximized, and ii) set SAhas color g1and SBhas color g2, i.e., g(SA)=g1andg(SB)=g2. Once we find SA,SBwe update the set U−removing the new covered element, U−←U−\(SA∪SB), and we add SA,SBinX. In the end, after covering all elements ( U−=∅), we return X. The pseudocode of our algorithm is shown in the technical report [14].

We run the standard greedy algorithm for the max k-cover problem. Let Y=U−be the current set of uncovered elements in U−and letC=∅be the family ofksets we return. The next steps are repeated until |C|=k orY=∅. In each iteration, the algorithm chooses the set S∈S− such that|S∩Y|is maximized. Having theoretically analyzed the proposed algorithms, in this section we experimentally evaluate the efficiency and efficacy of our algorithms on real and synthetic datasets. Datasets: We use 3 real datasets, one semi-synthesized, and one synthesized dataset to evaluate our methods. Our first set of ex- periments (§ 7.1 and § 7.2) are motivated by Example 1 (Team of Experts Formation), for which we use the Strategeion Resume Skills dataset1. It consists of 1986 rows as candidates with differ- ent skills. The skill of a candidate is shown as 218 binary columns each corresponding to one skill. As an AI Ethics benchmark, the dataset also contains demographic group information, including the (binary) gender. The male-to-female ratio in this dataset is 0.8. Motivated by the "Fair survey data collection" application demon- strated in § 2, we use two additional real datasets: Adult Income andCOMPAS (§ 7.3). The Adult Income Dataset [ 18] consists of demographic information for individuals, which was extracted from the 1994 Census database. The dataset is primarily used to predict whether a person earns more than $50,000 per year based on various attributes (14 columns and 48,842 rows). Gender is the sensitive attribute in this dataset. The COMPAS dataset [ 1] con- tains data used to evaluate the effectiveness and fairness of the COMPAS recidivism prediction algorithm. This dataset includes criminal history, jail and prison time, demographics, and COM- PAS risk scores for defendants from Broward County, Florida (52 columns and 18,316 rows), while race is the sensitive attribute. The third set of experiments (§ 7.4) are using the POPSIM [38] dataset. POPSIM is a semi-synthetic dataset that combines popu- lation statistics along with a geo-database. It is used to represent 1http://bit.ly/2SeS4xoindividual-level data with demographic information for the state of Illinois. Race is used as the sensitive attribute (5 groups). It contains 2,000,000 locations represented as points in R2. For the last set of experiments, (§ 7.5), we synthesized a dataset consisting of a number of points as ground set and a family of sub- sets with different coverage distributions on this ground set. More details about this dataset is provided in the technical report [14]. Algorithms: We compare four algorithms over all the experi- ments: Standard Greedy Set Cover (SC), Naive Algorithm (Naive), Fair Greedy Algorithm (AllPick), Efficient or Faster Fair Greedy Algorithm (EffAllPick). We also compare these algorithms with the optimum solution (using the brute-force algorithm for Standard Set Cover (Opt-SC) and a brute-force algorithm for Fair Set Cover (Opt-Fair)). These algorithms simply check all possible covers to find the best optimum solution. For the generalized version of the problem, we compared the General Fair Set Cover (GFSC) algo- rithm and the Efficient or Faster GFSC algorithm (EffGFSC) along with Naive and Standard Greedy (SC) algorithms. In this part, we used two real datasets Adult andCOMPAS. In the Adult dataset, the gender is the sensitive attribute. The female-to- male ratio is almost 0.5 in this dataset. We aim to select a subset of individuals (rows) from this dataset to form a set of candidates for a survey that is fair and covers a set of all 30 available criteria. For example, we want to have at least one individual with ’High Income’ and at least one with ’Low Income’. Similarly, we want to cover all categories of ’Marital Status’ in the final cover. These 30 criteria are our ground-set and the individuals are the family of sets that build the cover. The same procedure is followed for theCOMPAS dataset. We considered 3 races, "African-American," "Caucasian," and "Hispanic," as the demographic groups (colors) and defined a set of 30 criteria to satisfy in the final cover (i.e., the set of individuals chosen for a survey). We picked a sample of sizeMfrom the rows of these datasets. This sample corresponds to a set of individuals covering the ground set (the criteria). In other words,|S|=MwhereSis the family of subsets defined in the Set Cover problem. We repeated the experiments on different values ofM={2000,3000,..., 10000}. The results of these runs are illustrated in Fig 3 and in the technical report [ 14]. The results are similar to the previous experiment § 7.2. on POPSIM dataset. The x-axis shows different values of N(size of the ground set).

For example, Fig. 12 in the technical report [ 14] shows an example of a fair cover and an unfair cover on a sampled subset of this dataset. Each point is an individual, and each circle shows a selected individual and its coverage. Similar to the previous experiments, we ran our methods on different number of elements (size of ground set). In Fig 4, we show the output size, fairness and running time of the algorithms over different sizes of the ground set (from 0.25M to 2M). The algorithm AllPick did not finish within 1hour so we exclude it from the figure. All observations are the same as in the other datasets: Our EffAillPick algorithm satisfies zero-fairness and it is competitive to SC with respect to the size of the output cover and the running time. The SC algorithm returns highly unfair outputs with fairness ratio less than 0.2in most cases.

We use our synthetic data to verify our methods in different settings like Generalized Fair Set Cover and more demographic groups (colors). Due to space limitations, these experiments and the details of our synthetic datasets are provided in the technical report [ 14].

The Fair Team Formation Problem and the fair set cover problem with two groups are also discussed in [ 5]. The authors form a fair team of experts, covering a specific set of skills and, at the same time, being fair in terms of sensitive attributes. They focus on the binary case where individuals only belong to one of the two demographic groups. They present inapproximability results and some some heuristics. The practical experiments are limited to a dataset of around 6 skills and 1211 individuals.
